Grok Bot can already reason, browse, write code and run a computer. What it can't do is hear you.

The bottleneck on personal agents isn't intelligence anymore. It's context.

A lot of what we ask for in a day is said out loud. In a meeting, on a call, on a walk. None of it reaches the agent. We built agents that can do almost anything, then made them wait for us to type.

Speech is the highest-bandwidth input we have, and almost all of it disappears. A transcript keeps it. Every word, in order, something an agent can always go back to.

So we built a harness around the watch. You capture on your wrist. Our Moment MCP connects the full transcript to your Grok Bot. The harness turns it into action items, routes each one to the right tool, and points back to the exact moment it came from.

Grok Bot already knows how to do the work. We're allowing it to collect more context around you.

How SpaceXAI built Grok Bot in a month — and launched it to the public three weeks later.

Ever wondered how products like this actually get built? How AI becomes an assistant you can hand work to while you go do something else? Here’s how it happened.

It started with a handful of people sitting apart from the rest of the company. Their own corner of the office, private Slack channels, and one month to build a working prototype.

The team already had experience building coding agents. Now they needed a product that would work just as well for a recruiter or a coffee shop owner.

Two decisions formed the foundation: the agent runs in the cloud, and it gets its own computer. You send a task from your phone, close your laptop, and the work continues. Your device doesn’t need to stay on.

Why does AI need a computer at all? Because plenty of business tools don’t let software perform every necessary action through an API.

So Grok Bot has several ways to get things done: APIs, MCP connections to tools, and direct interaction with a website’s interface. Seeing the screen, clicking buttons, entering text. Just as a person would.

This is where some of the difficult engineering began. The agent’s mouse control wasn’t precise enough to click a particular element in Salesforce. One tiny miss could bring an entire task to a halt.

The team collected these failures and improved the underlying infrastructure: what the agent could see in the browser, how it perceived the screen, and how precisely it could interact with the interface. One measure of progress was whether a specific, previously blocked workflow finally worked.

Another key piece is memory. Bots retain context from past interactions and persist beyond a single session. You can assign a bot a role and gradually teach it your preferences, instead of copying background information from one chat to another.

Then users came up with the next layer themselves.

Employees initially created five to ten bots for different areas of work. Some then started “promoting” their best bot to chief of staff: they gave it the task, and it delegated work to the others. A lead assistant coordinating a team of agents.

Automations became conversational, too. You type “check this every morning,” and the bot sets it up. According to the team, 99% of automations on the platform were being created this way at the time of the interview.

Even skills — reusable instructions for bots — were something the team wanted users to stop having to manage. The idea was to create them in the background, without requiring people to learn special commands.

That first month produced an internal prototype. The next three weeks went into preparing it for public launch. The team personally onboarded a few hundred users while stripping unnecessary settings and technical details out of the interface.

The most interesting part is the workflows this enabled.

One recruiting example: visit a conference website every morning, download new research papers, identify previously untracked authors, add them to a spreadsheet, research their backgrounds, and check who inside the company could make an introduction.

One of the team’s own bots became a QA tester. They installed Grok Bot on its computer so it could test new versions of Grok Bot: run assigned workflows, record the results in Notion, and compare them with previous releases.

Yes, Grok Bot tests Grok Bot.

Another setup described in the interview brings the pieces together: an assistant monitors mentions of the product on X, combines that feedback with internal context, and works with the QA bot to see whether a reported bug can be reproduced.

For me, that’s the real wow moment. Behind a simple chat message, there can be an entire sequence: find information, understand the context, delegate a check to another bot, and come back with a result.

And it all depends on very concrete things: memory, a cloud computer, access to tools, and the ability to reliably complete every step of a task.

For the full story, I recommend watching the video attached to this post. The team goes deeper into how they built it and which decisions made the difference.

Someone asked me what the best moment of @Oracle AI World was.

It wasn’t the announcements, the puppies or the Cybertruck.

It was six words from a customer after my workshop.

“You’ve just changed everything for me.”

They had just sat through my session on agent memory in enterprise workloads, and that was their reaction. 

By far the best moment of the week for me. 
And the week had plenty of contenders:
loads of announcements
loads of puppies
a Cybertruck
a Tractor

Anyone who has built a workshop, or any teaching material, knows what the ideal outcome is.

The people in the room understand the content and it lands. 
When that happens, the hours spent building slides, checking the transitions are smooth, and working out how much detail to pack in all feel worth it.

Agent memory is one of the topics worth understanding properly right now. 
Personal AI assistants are arriving fast (Muse, Grok Bot, Dots), and every one of them depends on how it remembers you: what it stores, what it retrieves, what it forgets, and how it does all of that without burning through tokens. 

I teach this in my Maven class: Introduction to AI Agent Memory.
The moment where something clicks and changes how you think about agents isn’t reserved for a conference workshop. 

You can have it from your desk.

The course is rated 5⭐️, and here is what the first cohort said:

1️⃣ “Richmond breaks down the different types of memory, how agents can share context, and when to use a file system or a database. He also shows how vector search, RAG and reranking come together in a real memory pipeline.” (Mark, developer)

2️⃣ “Loved his deep dive and breakdown of the modes of conversational agents: Assistant, Workflow and Deep Research, and how agent memory plays a role in each.” (Sai, Cloud Solution Architect, Microsoft)

Next cohort is Thursday 5 November.

I won't pick a daily driver for my autonomous agent before I've tried @Claude Duet.

So far, I like @OpenAI Dot. It looks very promising, but it doesn't evolve much, at least from what I see, and it can't safely drive more than 2 or 3 sessions in parallel.

@Muse is surprisingly good and polished, maybe the most proactive of them all. But it doesn't feel built for work, and I don't need an agent to find me a hotel. I don't even let my wife do that.

Then there's Grok @bot. I have one for X, but I haven't gone deep with it. It was really dumb a few times at the beginning, and I lost the little trust I'd given it. The hype is real, though, and half of tech bro Twitter is rooting for it, including people I respect like @theo. It has to be good. I want to believe.

I still have a Hermes agent. I love it for research and for discussing ideas, not for doing the actual work. And I have an OpenClaw agent enjoying an early retirement. You can call it nostalgia. 6 months feels like a century in AI land.

Now, I have big hopes for Duet because, on paper, it's built for people like me: small business owners juggling way too many balls. Like OpenAI Dot, it would have access to my repos, hundreds of sessions, skills, plugins and historical data. An agent needs context, and seriously good access to Codex and Claude.

To make up my mind while waiting for Duet, I'm closely following a few people who build these projects or have real influence on them. An agent, alone or running a swarm, takes time to set up properly in your ecosystem before it gives its best, and I don't have the bandwidth to do that 2 or 3 times.

We are back to the Android vs iOS thing, where you definitely need to pick a side if you want the best of it.

If you are in a similar situation and don't follow them yet, start here: @ahuja_karan, @gabemulley, @embirico, @TheRohanVarma, @christinesed, @dps, @poteto (of course!) and @romanugarte.
